title: Arrays: Declaration, Indexing, Size, and Dynamic Alternatives
description: How fixed-size arrays and their dynamic collection alternatives compare across the three languages.
objectives: Compare dynamic, resizable alternatives to fixed arrays

content.heading: Python
content.body: Python has no separate, fixed-size 'array' type in everyday use — list serves that role and is dynamically resizable by default (append, insert, remove all work in place). Indexing out of range raises IndexError, a caught, well-defined exception, not silent memory corruption. For genuinely fixed-size, homogeneous numeric arrays, the array module or NumPy exist, but list covers the vast majority of everyday use.

content.heading: Java
content.body: Arrays (int[] arr = new int[5];) are fixed-size once created, with a .length field, and bounds-checked at runtime — an out-of-range access throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, a caught exception, not memory corruption. For resizable collections, ArrayList<T> (backed internally by a resizable array) is the standard dynamic alternative.

content.heading: C
content.body: Arrays (int arr[5];) are fixed-size, with no built-in length tracking (sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) works only in the declaring scope, before any decay) and absolutely no bounds checking — an out-of-range access is undefined behavior, silently corrupting memory rather than raising any error. There is no built-in dynamic array type at all; achieving resizable behavior requires manually managing a heap-allocated buffer with malloc/realloc.

content.heading: Key Differences
content.body: Both Python's list and Java's arrays are bounds-checked, raising a clear, catchable error on out-of-range access; C provides zero bounds checking, making out-of-range access a silent, potentially serious bug rather than a caught error. Python's list is dynamically resizable by default; Java requires ArrayList (or similar) for resizability, since its arrays are fixed; C has no built-in resizable array type at all.

content.heading: When It Matters
content.body: This is one of the most consequential safety differences in the whole comparison: an off-by-one array bug in Python or Java surfaces immediately as a clear exception; the same bug in C can silently corrupt memory and manifest as a confusing crash (or security vulnerability) much later, far from its actual cause.

keyPoints: Python's list and Java's arrays are both bounds-checked, raising clear exceptions on out-of-range access
C performs no bounds checking at all — out-of-range access is undefined behavior, not a caught error
Python's list is dynamically resizable by default; Java needs ArrayList; C has no built-in resizable array type
